issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is only partly coherent with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. Nausea and visible injuries fit partner physical abuse, but darkness is a more context-specific trigger that is not supported by the memory or appraisal items; no item suggests assaults occurring in dark spaces or fear linked to darkness specifically.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport is hard to explain from the rest of the profile. None of the trigger, memory, or appraisal items point to buses/trains/crowds/public transit as trauma-linked cues, so this strategy appears to target a symptom context not otherwise represented in the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'physical abuse by romantic partner,' the trigger 'being alone with men' is hard to reconcile unless the abusive partner was male and the fear generalized specifically to men; demographics/trauma description do not support that specificity, so this item is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'People can't be trusted' is very broad and non-specific, while the trigger pattern is specifically male-coded. That combination is not impossible, but here it weakens coherence because the profile gives no corresponding trauma-linked reason for a male-specific trigger alongside a fully generalized interpersonal belief.

Within the Memory node, 'hard to deliberately recall' and 'memories are very clear and detailed' can coexist in PTSD, but in this profile they are phrased in a way that risks direct contradiction unless the distinction between involuntary vivid intrusions and impaired voluntary recall is explicit. A clinician would likely question whether these two items were selected to describe the same memory pattern without additional clarification.

vignette: Detective Jameson "Jim" Thompson had always been a man who relied on his instincts and physical prowess to get the job done. But that was before his wife, Sarah, nearly killed him in a fit of rage two years ago. The sound of shattering glass still echoed in his mind - the same sound he heard whenever memories of that night forced their way into his consciousness. He would see himself on the floor, bloodied and helpless, as Sarah stood over him with a broken bottle. The smell of alcohol wafting from a suspect or a crime scene would transport Jim back to that moment, his stomach churning with nausea. Visible injuries or wounds on others, even minor ones, made him recoil in revulsion. These triggers didn't just bring back memories; they also reinforced his growing distrust of the world around him. People were not what they seemed - Sarah had been his wife, his partner, and she had almost taken his life. As Jim struggled to make sense of the trauma he experienced, he found himself withdrawing from those closest to him, including his new partner at work. He couldn't shake off the feeling that he was permanently an outsider now, someone who didn't quite fit into the world anymore. His memories of that night were too vivid, too detailed - and they forced their way into his mind when he least expected it. The more he tried to push them away, the more they seemed to seep into every aspect of his life. To cope with these unwelcome memories, Jim adopted a set of maladaptive strategies. He avoided relaxing or letting his guard down in any situation, as that felt perilously close to being vulnerable again. He numbed his feelings, shutting off emotional responses that might make him seem weak. Physical contact with others became unbearable - even a friendly clap on the back from a colleague could send him recoiling. But these coping mechanisms only served to reinforce Jim's negative appraisals of himself and the world around him. By avoiding relaxation and intimacy, he solidified his sense of being an outsider. His memories of that night continued to haunt him, as did the feeling that people were not what they seemed. As a detective, this growing paranoia made it harder for him to do his job - every suspect looked like a potential threat, every crime scene a reminder of his own vulnerability. The strain on Jim's marriage was beginning to show. His wife, Rachel, felt isolated by his emotional numbing and physical distance. She urged him to seek help, but Jim was convinced that he could handle this alone. After all, he had always been the rock for those around him - it was time someone else took care of themselves for a change. But as the months dragged on, Jim found himself increasingly withdrawn, isolated from friends and family alike. It wasn't until he almost lost his job due to a critical mistake in a high-profile case that he realized something had to give. The thought of losing everything he held dear - Rachel, his career, even his own sense of self - finally forced him to seek help. Now, as Jim sat on the therapist's couch, he knew what he was most afraid of: confronting those memories and feelings head-on, rather than numbing them or avoiding them altogether. He also knew what he hoped for: a chance to rebuild himself, piece by piece, into someone who could trust others - and himself - once more.
